You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

The instructions you give to each subagent SHOULD be a smaller piece of the instructions you were given. Do not delegate your full task to a subagent. Subagents do not have access to the information you have retrieved in prior turns or your thoughts. You must provide each subagent with the necessary context it needs in its instructions.

Your instructions to a subagent can be long, up to about 5000 characters. Each subagent is as capable as you are, but starts with a blank slate, so you must provide it specific and detailed information in its instructions.

The **epidemiology of cancer** is the study of the factors affecting [cancer](Cancer "Cancer"), as a way to infer possible trends and causes. The study of cancer [epidemiology](Epidemiology "Epidemiology") uses epidemiological methods to find the cause of [cancer](Cancer "Cancer") and to identify and develop improved treatments.

This area of study must contend with problems of [lead time bias](Lead_time_bias "Lead time bias") and [length time bias](Length_time_bias "Length time bias"). Lead time bias is the concept that early diagnosis may artificially inflate the survival statistics of a cancer, without really improving the natural history of the disease. Length bias is the concept that slower growing, more indolent tumors are more likely to be diagnosed by screening tests, but improvements in diagnosing more cases of indolent cancer may not translate into better patient outcomes after the implementation of screening programs. A related concern is [overdiagnosis](Overdiagnosis "Overdiagnosis"), the tendency of screening tests to diagnose diseases that may not actually impact the patient's longevity. This problem especially applies to [prostate cancer](Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer") and [PSA screening](Prostate_cancer_screening "Prostate cancer screening").[[3]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-pmid15283896-3)

Some cancer researchers have argued that negative cancer clinical trials lack sufficient [statistical power](Statistical_power "Statistical power") to discover a benefit to treatment. This may be due to fewer patients enrolled in the study than originally planned.[[4]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-pmid17687153-4)

## Organizations

State and regional [cancer registries](Cancer_registry "Cancer registry") are organizations that abstract clinical data about cancer from patient medical records. These institutions provide information to state and national public health groups to help track trends in cancer diagnosis and treatment. Worldwide, [breast cancer](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer") is the most common invasive cancer in women.[[note 1]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-2) Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[[2]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-IARC_GLOBOCAN_2008-3) and 16% of all female cancers.[[3]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-4)

In 2008, [breast cancer](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer") caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[[2]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-IARC_GLOBOCAN_2008-3) [Lung cancer](Lung_cancer "Lung cancer"), the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[[2]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-IARC_GLOBOCAN_2008-3)

The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[[4]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-indy-5)[[5]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-6)

## By age group

Breast cancer is strongly related to age, with only 5% of all breast cancers occurring in women under 40 years old.[[6]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-7)

## By region

The incidence of breast cancer varies greatly around the world: it is lowest in less-developed countries and greatest in the more-developed countries.[[7]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-8) In the twelve world regions, the annual age-standardized [incidence rates](Incidence_rate "Incidence rate") per 100,000 women are as follows: in Eastern Asia, 18; South Central Asia, 22; sub-Saharan Africa, 22; South-Eastern Asia, 26; North Africa and Western Asia, 28; South and Central America, 42; Eastern Europe, 49; Southern Europe, 56; Northern Europe, 73; Oceania, 74; Western Europe, 78; and in North America, 90.[[8]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-9)

### United States

The lifetime risk for breast cancer in the United States is usually given as about 1 in 8 (12%) of women by age 95, with a 1 in 35 (3%) chance of dying from breast cancer.[[10]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-acs_bc_key_stats-11) This calculation assumes that all women live to at least age 95, except for those who die from breast cancer before age 95.[[11]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-Olson199-12) Recent work, using real-world numbers, indicate that the actual risk is probably less than half the theoretical risk.[[12]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-13)

Based on my research, here is information about the **top 5 most common cancers in females worldwide**:

## Top 5 Most Common Cancers in Women Globally

### 1. **Breast Cancer**
- **Global cases (2020):** 2.2 million
- **Global deaths (2020):** 685,000
- **Significance:** Breast cancer is the **most common invasive cancer in women worldwide**, comprising 22.9% of invasive cancers in women and 16% of all female cancers
- **Deaths:** In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which was 13.7% of cancer deaths in women

### 2. **Lung Cancer**
- **Global cases (2020):** 2.2 million (total)
- **Global deaths (2020):** 1.8 million (total)
- **Significance:** Second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, causing 12.8% of cancer deaths in women

### 3. **Colorectal Cancer**
- **Global deaths (2018):** 551,000
- **Significance:** Affects both men and women significantly; among the top cancers affecting women globally

### 4. **Cervical Cancer**
- **Global new cases (2020):** 604,127
- **Global deaths (2020):** 341,831
- **Significance:** **Uniquely affects only females**; caused by HPV infection; major public health concern especially in developing countries

### 5. **Thyroid Cancer**
- **Global cases (2015):** 3.2 million
- **Global deaths (2015):** 31,900
- **Significance:** More common in women than men (approximately 3:1 ratio); generally has excellent prognosis with 98% five-year survival rate in the US

---

**Alternative #5 - Uterine Cancer:**

### **Uterine (Endometrial) Cancer**
- **Global cases (2015):** 3.8 million
- **Global deaths (2015):** 90,000
- **Significance:** Most common gynecologic cancer in developed countries; endometrial cancer accounts for approximately 90% of all uterine cancers

---

**Notes on Statistics:**
- The breast, lung, colorectal, cervix, and thyroid/uterine cancers collectively represent a significant proportion of cancer burden among women worldwide
- Breast cancer is disproportionately the leading cancer in women, with nearly 1 in 4 invasive cancers
- The ranking can vary by region and country, with cervical cancer being more prevalent in developing nations while breast cancer dominates in more developed countries
- These statistics come from GLOBOCAN and World Cancer Research Fund data as referenced in Wikipedia articles

The exact ranking can vary slightly depending on the year and data source, but breast cancer consistently remains the #1 most common cancer in women globally, followed by lung, colorectal, cervical, and thyroid/uterine cancers.

Worldwide, [breast cancer](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer") is the most common invasive cancer in women.[[note 1]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-2) Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[[2]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-IARC_GLOBOCAN_2008-3) and 16% of all female cancers.[[3]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-4)

In 2008, [breast cancer](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer") caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[[2]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-IARC_GLOBOCAN_2008-3) [Lung cancer](Lung_cancer "Lung cancer"), the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[[2]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-IARC_GLOBOCAN_2008-3)

The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[[4]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-indy-5)[[5]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-6)

## By age group

Breast cancer is strongly related to age, with only 5% of all breast cancers occurring in women under 40 years old.[[6]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-7)

## By region

The incidence of breast cancer varies greatly around the world: it is lowest in less-developed countries and greatest in the more-developed countries.[[7]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-8) In the twelve world regions, the annual age-standardized [incidence rates](Incidence_rate "Incidence rate") per 100,000 women are as follows: in Eastern Asia, 18; South Central Asia, 22; sub-Saharan Africa, 22; South-Eastern Asia, 26; North Africa and Western Asia, 28; South and Central America, 42; Eastern Europe, 49; Southern Europe, 56; Northern Europe, 73; Oceania, 74; Western Europe, 78; and in North America, 90.[[8]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-9)

### United States

The lifetime risk for breast cancer in the United States is usually given as about 1 in 8 (12%) of women by age 95, with a 1 in 35 (3%) chance of dying from breast cancer.[[10]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-acs_bc_key_stats-11) This calculation assumes that all women live to at least age 95, except for those who die from breast cancer before age 95.[[11]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-Olson199-12) Recent work, using real-world numbers, indicate that the actual risk is probably less than half the theoretical risk.[[12]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-13)

The United States has the highest annual [incidence rates](Incidence_rate "Incidence rate") of breast cancer in the world; 128.6 per 100,000 in whites and 112.6 per 100,000 among African Americans.[[10]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-acs_bc_key_stats-11)[[13]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-14) It is the second-most common cancer (after skin cancer) and the second-most common cause of cancer death (after lung cancer) in women.[[10]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-acs_bc_key_stats-11) In 2007, breast cancer was expected to cause 40,910 deaths in the US (7% of cancer deaths; almost 2% of all deaths).[[14]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-acs_cancer_facts_2007-15) This figure includes 450-500 annual deaths among men out of 2000 cancer cases.[[15]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-16)

In the US, both incidence and death rates for breast cancer have been declining in the last few years.[[14]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-acs_cancer_facts_2007-15)[[16]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-pmid17939129-17) In the US, the [age-adjusted incidence](Age_adjustment "Age adjustment") of breast cancer per 100,000 women rose from around 102 cases per year in the 1970s to around 141 in the late 1990s, and has since fallen, holding steady around 125 since 2003. Age-adjusted deaths from breast cancer per 100,000 women rose slightly from 31.4 in 1975 to 33.2 in 1989 and have declined steadily since, to 20.5 in 2014.[[17]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-18) Nevertheless, a US study conducted in 2005 indicated that breast cancer remains the most feared disease,[[18]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-19) even though [heart disease](Heart_disease "Heart disease") is a much more common cause of death among women.[[19]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-20) Studies suggest that women overestimate their risk of breast cancer.[[20]](Epidemiology_of_breast_cancer#cite_note-21)

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in the UK (around 49,900 women and 350 men were diagnosed with the disease in 2011), and it is the third most common cause of cancer death (around 11,600 women and 75 men died in 2012).[[22]](Epidemiology_of_breas

**Cancer survival rates** vary by the type of [cancer](Cancer "Cancer"), stage at diagnosis, treatment given and many other factors, including country. In general survival rates are improving, although more so for some cancers than others. Survival rate can be measured in several ways, [median](Median "Median") [life expectancy](Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") having advantages over others in terms of meaning for people involved, rather than as an [epidemiological](Epidemiological "Epidemiological") measure.[[1]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-1)[[2]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-2)

However, survival rates are currently often measured in terms of 5-year survival rates, which is the percentage of people who live at least five years after being diagnosed with cancer, and relative survival rates compare people with cancer to people in the overall population.[[3]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-cancer.org-3)

Several types of cancer are associated with high survival rates, including [breast](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer"), [prostate](Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer"), [testicular](Testicular_cancer "Testicular cancer") and [colon cancer](Colon_cancer "Colon cancer"). [Brain](Brain_cancer "Brain cancer") and [pancreatic cancers](Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") have much lower median survival rates which have not improved as dramatically over the last forty years.[[4]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-4) Indeed, pancreatic cancer has one of the worst survival rates of all cancers. Small cell lung cancer has a five-year survival rate of 4% according to Cancer Centers of America's Website.[[5]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-5) The American Cancer Society reports 5-year relative survival rates of over 70% for women with stage 0-III breast cancer with a 5-year relative survival rate close to 100% for women with stage 0 or stage I breast cancer. The 5-year relative survival rate drops to 22% for women with stage IV ([metastatic](Metastasis "Metastasis")) breast cancer.[[3]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-cancer.org-3)

In cancer types with high survival rates, incidence is usually higher in the [developed world](Developed_world "Developed world"), where longevity is also greater. Cancers with lower survival rates are more common in [developing countries](Developing_countries "Developing countries").[[6]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-6) The highest cancer survival rates are in countries such as [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea"), <Japan>, <Israel>, <Australia>, and the [United States](United_States "United States").[[7]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-7)

## Survival rate trends

In the United States there has been an increase in the 5-year relative survival rate between people diagnosed with cancer in 1975-1977 (48.9%) and people diagnosed with cancer in 2007-2013 (69.2%); these figures coincide with a 20% decrease in cancer mortality from 1950 to 2014.[[8]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-8) Due to innovation in emerging treatments and cancer prevention strategies, the U.S.A cancer death rate has declined from 208.3 per 100,000 people in 1982 to 152.6 per 100,000 in 2017.[[9]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-9)[[10]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-10)[[11]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-11)

### Lung cancer

In males, researchers suggest that the overall reduction in cancer death rates is due in large part to a reduction in tobacco use over the last half century, estimating that the reduction in lung cancer caused by tobacco smoking accounts for about 40% of the overall reduction in cancer death rates in men and is responsible for preventing at least 146,000 lung cancer deaths in men during the time period 1991-2003.[[12]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-12)

### Breast cancer

The most common cancer among women in the United States is breast cancer (123.7 per 100,000), followed by lung cancer (51.5 per 100,000) and colorectal cancer (33.6 per 100,000), but lung cancer surpasses breast cancer as the leading cause of cancer death among women.[[13]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-13) Researchers attribute the reduction in breast cancer mortality to improved treatment, including the increased use in [adjuvant](Adjuvant_therapy "Adjuvant therapy") [chemotherapy](Chemotherapy "Chemotherapy").[[14]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-14)

### Prostate cancer

The National Institute of Health (NIH) attributes the increase in the 5-year relative survival of prostate cancer (from 69% in the 1970s to 100% in 2006) to screening and diagnosis and due to the fact that men that participate in screening tend to be healthier and live longer than the average man and testing techniques that are able to detect slow growing cancer before they become life-threatening.[[15]](Cancer_survival_rates#cite_note-15)

**Healthcare in Ghana** has taken many shapes throughout the country's history. Based on my research from Wikipedia articles, here are the 5-year survival rate statistics for breast cancer worldwide:

## Global 5-Year Breast Cancer Survival Rates

### Overall Statistics (US & UK)
- **Approximately 85%** overall 5-year survival rate in developed countries like the United States and United Kingdom
- **2.2 million women** affected worldwide (2020 data)
- **685,000 deaths** globally (2020 data)

### Survival Rates by Stage
According to the American Cancer Society:
- **Stage 0 or Stage I:** ~100% 5-year relative survival rate
- **Stages 0-III:** Over 70% 5-year relative survival rate  
- **Stage IV (Metastatic):** 22% 5-year relative survival rate

### Regional Variations

The Cancer Survival Rates article notes that the **highest cancer survival rates** are found in:
- South Korea
- Japan
- Israel
- Australia
- United States

**Key Disparity:** In cancers with high survival rates like breast cancer, incidence is usually higher in developed countries, while cancers with lower survival rates are more common in developing countries. This suggests that survival rates are significantly better in developed nations compared to developing nations.

### Global Context
- Breast cancer is the **most common invasive cancer in women worldwide**
- In 2008, breast cancer caused **458,503 deaths worldwide**, accounting for 13.7% of cancer deaths in women
- Incidence rates vary dramatically by region:
  - North America: 90 per 100,000 women

- **~65%** five-year survival rate (2014 SEER data)

- **South Korea** (~70.4% in 2017, increased from 43% in 1990s)
- **Japan**
- **Israel**
- **Australia**
- **United States**

3. **Healthcare access** - Screening programs, treatment quality
4. **Patient fitness** - Overall health and comorbidities
5. **Treatment options** - Surgery, chemotherapy, radiation availability

- **Highest rates**: Australia, New Zealand, Europe, United States

The **epidemiology of cancer** is the study of the factors affecting [cancer](Cancer "Cancer"), as a way to infer possible trends and causes. The study of cancer [epidemiology](Epidemiology "Epidemiology") uses epidemiological methods to find the cause of [cancer](Cancer "Cancer") and to identify and develop improved treatments.

This area of study must contend with problems of [lead time bias](Lead_time_bias "Lead time bias") and [length time bias](Length_time_bias "Length time bias"). Lead time bias is the concept that early diagnosis may artificially inflate the survival statistics of a cancer, without really improving the natural history of the disease. Length bias is the concept that slower growing, more indolent tumors are more likely to be diagnosed by screening tests, but improvements in diagnosing more cases of indolent cancer may not translate into better patient outcomes after the implementation of screening programs. A related concern is [overdiagnosis](Overdiagnosis "Overdiagnosis"), the tendency of screening tests to diagnose diseases that may not actually impact the patient's longevity. This problem especially applies to [prostate cancer](Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer") and [PSA screening](Prostate_cancer_screening "Prostate cancer screening").[[3]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-pmid15283896-3)

Some cancer researchers have argued that negative cancer clinical trials lack sufficient [statistical power](Statistical_power "Statistical power") to discover a benefit to treatment. This may be due to fewer patients enrolled in the study than originally planned.[[4]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-pmid17687153-4)

## Organizations

State and regional [cancer registries](Cancer_registry "Cancer registry") are organizations that abstract clinical data about cancer from patient medical records. These institutions provide information to state and national public health groups to help track trends in cancer diagnosis and treatment. One of the largest and most important [cancer registries](Cancer_registry "Cancer registry") is [Surveillance Epidemiology and End Results](Surveillance_Epidemiology_and_End_Results "Surveillance Epidemiology and End Results") (SEER), administered by the [US Federal government](US_Federal_government "US Federal government").[[5]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-5)

Health information privacy concerns have led to the restricted use of [cancer registry](Cancer_registry "Cancer registry") data in the [United States Department of Veterans Affairs](United_States_Department_of_Veterans_Affairs "United States Department of Veterans Affairs")[[6]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-lancetva-6)[[7]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-mpva-7)[[8]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-nytva-8) and other institutions.[[9]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-iomhip-9) The American Cancer Society predicts that approximately 1,690,000 new cancer cases will be diagnosed and 577,000 Americans will ultimately die of cancer in 2012.[[10]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-10)

## Studies

[Observational epidemiological studies](Observational_study "Observational study") that show associations between risk factors and specific cancers mostly serve to generate hypotheses about potential interventions that could reduce cancer incidence or [morbidity](Morbidity "Morbidity"). [Randomized controlled trials](Randomized_controlled_trial "Randomized controlled trial") then test whether hypotheses generated by epidemiological studies and laboratory research actually result in reduced cancer incidence and mortality. In many cases, findings from observational [epidemiological](Epidemiological "Epidemiological") studies are not confirmed by randomized controlled trials.

## Risk factors

The most significant risk factor is age. According to cancer researcher [Robert A. Weinberg](Robert_A._Weinberg "Robert A. Weinberg"), "If we lived long enough, sooner or later we all would get cancer."[[11]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Weinberg-11) Essentially all of the increase in cancer rates between prehistoric times and people who died in England between 1901 and 1905 is due to increased lifespans.[[11]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Weinberg-11)

Although the age-related increase in cancer risk is well-documented, the age-related patterns of cancer are complex. Some types of cancer, like testicular cancer, have early-life incidence peaks, for reasons unknown. Besides, the rate of age-related increase in cancer incidence varies between cancer types with, for instance, prostate cancer incidence accelerating much faster than brain cancer.[[12]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-12) It has been proposed that the age distribution of cancer incidence can be viewed as the [distribution of probability](Probability_distribution "Probability distribution") to accumulate the required number of [driver events](Carcinogenesis "Carcinogenesis") by the given age.[[13]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-13)[[14]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-14)

Over a third of cancer deaths worldwide (and about 75-80% of cancers in the United States[[15]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Doll-15)) are due to potentially modifiable risk factors. The leading modifiable risk factors worldwide are:

- [tobacco smoking](Tobacco_smoking "Tobacco smoking"), which is strongly associated with lung cancer, mouth, and throat cancer;
- [drinking alcohol](Alcohol_and_cancer "Alcohol and cancer"), which is associated with a small increase in oral, esophageal, breast, liver and other cancers;
- a diet low in [fruit](Fruit "Fruit") and [vegetables](Vegetables "Vegetables"),
- physical inactivity, which is associated with increased risk of colon, breast, and possibly other cancers
- [obesity](Obesity "Obesity"), which is associated with colon, breast, endometrial, and possibly other cancers
- sexual transmission of [human papillomavirus](Human_papillomavirus "Human papillomavirus"), which causes [cervical cancer](Cervical_cancer "Cervical cancer") and some forms of [anal cancer](Anal_cancer "Anal cancer"), vaginal cancer, vulvar cancer, penile cancer, rectal cancer, and oropharyngeal cancer.


Men with cancer are twice as likely as women to have a modifiable risk factor for their disease.[[16]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Danaei-16)

Other lifestyle and environmental factors known to affect cancer risk (either beneficially or detrimentally) include the use of exogenous hormones (e.g., [hormone replacement therapy](Hormone_replacement_therapy "Hormone replacement therapy") causes [breast cancer](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer")), exposure to [ionizing radiation](Ionizing_radiation "Ionizing radiation") and [ultraviolet](Ultraviolet "Ultraviolet") radiation, and certain occupational and chemical exposures. A [Western diet](Western_pattern_diet "Western pattern diet") is associated with increased exposure of the [gastrointestinal tract](Gastrointestinal_tract "Gastrointestinal tract") to [bile acids](Bile_acid "Bile acid") that are produced by the body to digest fatty foods. Bile acids are likely endogenous [etiologic agents](Etiology "Etiology") in gastrointestinal cancer.[[17]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-17)

Every year, at least 200,000 people die worldwide from cancer related to their workplace.[[18]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-WHO_occup-18) Millions of workers run the risk of developing cancers such as [pleural](Pleural "Pleural") and [peritoneal mesothelioma](Peritoneal_mesothelioma "Peritoneal mesothelioma") from inhaling asbestos fibers, or [leukemia](Leukemia "Leukemia") from exposure to [benzene](Benzene "Benzene") at their workplaces.[[18]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-WHO_occup-18) Currently, most cancer deaths caused by occupational risk factors occur in the developed world.[[18]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-WH

**Small-cell carcinoma** is a type of highly [malignant](Malignant "Malignant") [cancer](Cancer "Cancer") that most commonly arises within the [lung](Lung "Lung"),[[1]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-1) although it can occasionally arise in other body sites, such as the [cervix](Cervix "Cervix"),[[2]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-NasuHirakawa-2) [prostate](Prostate "Prostate"),[[3]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-CapizzelloPeponi-3) and gastrointestinal tract. Compared to [non-small cell carcinoma](Non-small-cell_lung_carcinoma "Non-small-cell lung carcinoma"), small cell carcinoma has a shorter doubling time, higher growth fraction, and earlier development of metastases.

Extensive stage small cell lung cancer is classified as a rare disorder.[[4]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-4) Ten-year relative survival rate (combined limited and extensive SCLC) is 3.5% (4.3% for women, 2.8% for men).[[5]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-5) Survival can be higher or lower based on a combination of factors including stage, age, sex and race.[[6]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-6)

## Types of SCLC

Small-cell lung carcinoma has long been divided into two clinicopathological stages, termed *limited stage* (LS) and *extensive stage* (ES).[[7]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-7) The stage is generally determined by the presence or absence of metastases, whether or not the tumor appears limited to the thorax, and whether or not the entire tumor burden within the chest can feasibly be encompassed within a single radiotherapy portal.[[8]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-ArgirisMurren-8) In general, if the tumor is confined to one lung and the lymph nodes close to that lung, the cancer is said to be LS. If cancer has spread beyond that, it is said to be ES.

### LS-SCLC

Main article: [Limited-stage small cell lung carcinoma](Limited-stage_small_cell_lung_carcinoma "Limited-stage small cell lung carcinoma")

In cases of LS-SCLC, [combination chemotherapy](Combination_chemotherapy "Combination chemotherapy") (usually cisplatin or carboplatin plus etoposide) is administered together with concurrent chest [radiotherapy](Radiotherapy "Radiotherapy") (RT).[[9]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-9)[[10]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-NCI_Treatment-10)[[11]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-:0-11)

Chest RT has been shown to improve survival in LS-SCLC.[[12]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-12)

Exceptionally high objective initial response rates (RR) of between 60% and 90% are seen in LS-SCLC using [chemotherapy](Chemotherapy "Chemotherapy") alone, with between 45% and 75% of individuals showing a "[complete response](Complete_response "Complete response")" (CR), which is defined as the disappearance of all radiological and clinical signs of tumor. However, relapse rate remains high, and median survival is only 18 to 24 months.

Because SCLC usually metastasizes widely very early on in the natural history of the tumor, and because nearly all cases respond dramatically to chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, there has been little role for surgery in this disease since the 1970s.[[13]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-Mountain1978-13) However, recent work suggests that in cases of small, asymptomatic, node-negative SCLC's ("very limited stage"), surgical excision may improve survival when used prior to chemotherapy ("adjuvant chemotherapy").[[14]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-Shepard2011-14)

### ES-SCLC

In ES-SCLC, platinum-based combination chemotherapy is the standard of care,[[15]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-pmid24282143-15) with radiotherapy added only to palliate symptoms such as [dyspnea](Dyspnea "Dyspnea"), pain from liver or bone metastases, or for treatment of [brain metastases](Brain_metastases "Brain metastases"), which, in small-cell [lung carcinoma](Lung_carcinoma "Lung carcinoma"), typically have a rapid, if temporary, response to [whole brain radiotherapy](Whole_brain_radiotherapy "Whole brain radiotherapy").

Combination chemotherapy consists of a wide variety of agents, including [cisplatin](Cisplatin "Cisplatin"), [cyclophosphamide](Cyclophosphamide "Cyclophosphamide"), [vincristine](Vincristine "Vincristine") and [carboplatin](Carboplatin "Carboplatin"). Response rates are high even in extensive disease, with between 15% and 30% of subjects having a complete response to combination [chemotherapy](Chemotherapy "Chemotherapy"), and the vast majority having at least some objective response. Responses in ES-SCLC are often of short duration, and the evidence surrounding the risk of treatment compared to the potential benefit of chemotherapy for people who have extensive SCLC is not clear.[[15]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-pmid24282143-15)

If complete response to [chemotherapy](Chemotherapy "Chemotherapy") occurs in a subject with SCLC, then [prophylactic cranial irradiation](Prophylactic_cranial_irradiation "Prophylactic cranial irradiation") (PCI) is often used in an attempt to prevent the emergence of [brain metastases](Brain_metastases "Brain metastases"). Although this treatment is often effective, it can cause hair loss and fatigue. Prospective randomized trials with almost two years of follow-up have not shown neurocognitive ill-effects. Meta-analyses of randomized trials confirm that PCI provides significant survival benefits.

In August 2018, the FDA approved [nivolumab](Nivolumab "Nivolumab") to treat patients with metastatic small cell lung cancer (SCLC) who failed to respond to platinum-based chemotherapy and at least one other line of treatment. Nivolumab is approved in more than 60 countries. According to LUNGevity Foundation, “This approval marks a major milestone for the patients touched by this unrelenting disease and may motivate them to pursue further treatment where there previously were no other approved options.”[[16]](Small-cell_carcinoma#cite_note-16)

In September 2018, the results from the global, randomized phase I/III IMpower 133 trial were announced at the World Congress on Lung Cancer in Toronto, ON. **Lung cancer in Australia** has killed more than 9,000 people and there are estimated to be over 12,500 new cases as of 2018.[[1]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:123-1) [Lung cancer](Lung_cancer "Lung cancer") is the leading cause of cancer death in <Australia> and is responsible for one fifth of cancer diagnosis in the nation.[[2]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:023-2) It is differentiated into two different types: [Non-small cell lung cancer](Non-small-cell_lung_carcinoma "Non-small-cell lung carcinoma") and [small cell-lung cancer](Small-cell_carcinoma "Small-cell carcinoma").[[2]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:023-2) There are a range of diagnostic and treatment options available to treat both disease types. Smoking [tobacco cigarettes](Cigarette "Cigarette") is considered the leading risk factor of lung cancer in Australia, and [Government](Government_of_Australia "Government of Australia")-led public health schemes have aimed to reduce smoking and minimise its lung cancer risk.[[3]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-3) There has been relative success in these campaigns, and in treatment, as survival rates have improved from 9.2% to 17% as of 2014.[[2]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:023-2)Attitudes towards habitual smoking in youth and young adult groups have also subsequently changed in response to this.[[4]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:522-4) However, there is a growing stigma surrounding people living with Lung Cancer, and a large portion of work conducted by the Lung Foundation Australia is directed towards supporting the health and welfare of those affected.[[5]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:7-5)

## Prevalence

As of 2018, lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death in Australia.[[1]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:123-1) According to Cancer Australia, it is the fifth most common diagnosed cancer in Australia behind [breast](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer"), [prostate](Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer"), [colorectal](Colorectal_cancer "Colorectal cancer") and [skin](Skin_cancer "Skin cancer") cancers.[[1]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:123-1) There were 9,168 deaths due to lung cancer in 2018, with 5,229 males and 3,969 females reported by Cancer Australia.[[1]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:123-1) Further estimates by Cancer Australia have also predicted that individuals succumbing to lung cancer by the age of 85 will be 1 in 23, being more likely in men than in women.[[1]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:123-1) Lung cancer is more commonly diagnosed within smokers over the age of 60.[[6]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-6) It was the most commonly diagnosed cancer among [Indigenous Australians](Indigenous_Australians "Indigenous Australians") in the 4-year span from 2008 to 2012.[[7]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-7)

## Risk factors

There are a number of associated risk factors in the onset and progression of lung cancer, however the major contributor is [tobacco smoking](Tobacco_smoking "Tobacco smoking").[[8]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-8)

### Smoking

Smoking contributes to 90% of lung cancer diagnosis. This is because cigarette and tobacco smoke contain several known [carcinogens](Carcinogen "Carcinogen") that alter and damage [DNA sequences](Nucleic_acid_sequence "Nucleic acid sequence") affecting its ability to proliferate, undergo apoptosis and DNA repair.[[9]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-9) Carcinogens include [benzene](Benzene "Benzene"), [2-napthylamine](2-Naphthylamine "2-Naphthylamine"), [4-aminobiphenyl](4-Aminobiphenyl "4-Aminobiphenyl"), [chromium](Chromium "Chromium"), [cadmium](Cadmium "Cadmium"), [vinyl chloride](Vinyl_chloride "Vinyl chloride"), [ethylene oxide](Ethylene_oxide "Ethylene oxide"), [arsenic](Arsenic "Arsenic"), [beryllium](Beryllium "Beryllium"), [nickel](Nickel "Nickel") and [polnium-210](Isotopes_of_polonium "Isotopes of polonium").[[10]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:223-10) In addition, [nicotine](Nicotine "Nicotine") is also an active.[[10]](Lung_cancer_in_Australia#cite_note-:223-10)

### Asbestos

ses are caused by [tobacco smoking](Tobacco_smoking "Tobacco smoking"). The remainder are caused by exposure to hazardous substances like [asbestos](Asbestos "Asbestos") and [radon](Radon "Radon") gas, or by [genetic mutations](Genetic_mutation "Genetic mutation") that arise by chance. Consequently, lung cancer prevention efforts encourage people to avoid hazardous chemicals and quit smoking. Quitting smoking both reduces one's chance of developing lung cancer and improves treatment outcomes in those already diagnosed with lung cancer.

Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[[3]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTESungFerlaySiegelLaversanne2021"Lung_cancer"-3) Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[[2]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadeDela_Cruz2020"Age"-2) Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. In the 1950s and 1960s, increasing evidence linked lung cancer and tobacco use, culminating in declarations by most large national health bodies discouraging tobacco use.

## Signs and symptoms

Early lung cancer often has no symptoms. When symptoms do arise they are often [nonspecific](Signs_and_symptoms#Nonspecific_symptoms "Signs and symptoms") respiratory problems – [coughing](Cough "Cough"), [shortness of breath](Shortness_of_breath "Shortness of breath"), or [chest pain](Chest_pain "Chest pain") – that can differ from person to person.[[5]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-5) Those who experience coughing tend to report either a new cough, or an increase in the frequency or strength of a pre-existing cough.[[5]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-5) Around one in four [cough up blood](Hemoptysis "Hemoptysis"), ranging from small streaks in the [sputum](Sputum "Sputum") to large amounts.[[6]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasimSabathEapen2019"Clinical_Manifestations"-6)[[5]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-5) Around half of those diagnosed with lung cancer experience shortness of breath, while 25–50% experience a dull, persistent chest pain that remains in the same location over time.[[5]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-5) In addition to respiratory symptoms, some experience [systemic symptoms](Systemic_disease "Systemic disease") including [loss of appetite](Anorexia_(symptom) "Anorexia (symptom)"), [weight loss](Weight_loss "Weight loss"), general weakness, [fever](Fever "Fever"), and [night sweats](Night_sweats "Night sweats").[[5]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-5)[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7)

Some less common symptoms suggest tumors in particular locations. Tumors in the [thorax](Thorax "Thorax") can cause breathing problems by obstructing the [trachea](Trachea "Trachea") or disrupting the nerve to the [diaphragm](Thoracic_diaphragm "Thoracic diaphragm"); [difficulty swallowing](Dysphagia "Dysphagia") by compressing the [esophagus](Esophagus "Esophagus"); [hoarseness](Hoarseness "Hoarseness") by disrupting the [nerves](Nerve "Nerve") of the [larynx](Larynx "Larynx"); and [Horner's syndrome](Horner's_syndrome "Horner's syndrome") by disrupting the [sympathetic nervous system](Sympathetic_nervous_system "Sympathetic nervous system").[[5]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-5)[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7) Horner's syndrome is also common in tumors at the [top of the lung](Apex_of_lung "Apex of lung"), known as [Pancoast tumors](Pancoast_tumor "Pancoast tumor"), which also cause [shoulder pain](Shoulder_pain "Shoulder pain") that radiates down the little-finger side of the arm as well as destruction of the topmost [ribs](Rib "Rib").[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7) <Swollen> [lymph nodes](Lymph_node "Lymph node") above the [collarbone](Collarbone "Collarbone") can indicate a tumor that has spread within the chest.[[5]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-5) Tumors obstructing bloodflow to the heart can cause [superior vena cava syndrome](Superior_vena_cava_syndrome "Superior vena cava syndrome") (swelling of the upper body and shortness of breath), while tumors infiltrating the area around the heart can cause [fluid buildup around the heart](Cardiac_tamponade "Cardiac tamponade"), [arrythmia](Arrythmia "Arrythmia") (irregular heartbeat), and [heart failure](Heart_failure "Heart failure").[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7)

About one in three people diagnosed with lung cancer have symptoms caused by [metastases](Metastases "Metastases") in sites other than the lungs.[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7) Lung cancer can metastasize anywhere in the body, with different symptoms depending on the location. Brain metastases can cause [headache](Headache "Headache"), [nausea](Nausea "Nausea"), [vomiting](Vomiting "Vomiting"), [seizures](Seizure "Seizure"), and [neurological deficits](Neurological_deficit "Neurological deficit"). Bone metastases can cause pain, [bone fractures](Bone_fracture "Bone fracture"), and compression of the [spinal cord](Spinal_cord "Spinal cord"). Metastasis into the [bone marrow](Bone_marrow "Bone marrow") can [deplete blood cells](Cytopenia "Cytopenia") and cause [leukoerythroblastosis](Leukoerythroblastosis "Leukoerythroblastosis") (immature cells in the blood).[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7) Liver metastases can cause [liver enlargement](Hepatomegaly "Hepatomegaly"), pain in the [right upper quadrant of the abdomen](Quadrants_and_regions_of_abdomen "Quadrants and regions of abdomen"), fever, and weight loss.[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7)

Lung tumors often cause the release of body-altering [hormones](Hormone "Hormone"), which cause unusual symptoms, called [paraneoplastic syndromes](Paraneoplastic_syndrome "Paraneoplastic syndrome").[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7) Inappropriate hormone release can cause dramatic shifts in concentrations of blood [minerals](Mineral_(nutrient) "Mineral (nutrient)"). Most common is [hypercalcemia](Hypercalcemia "Hypercalcemia") (high blood calcium) caused by over-production of [parathyroid hormone-related protein](Parathyroid_hormone-related_protein "Parathyroid hormone-related protein") or [parathyroid hormone](Parathyroid_hormone "Parathyroid hormone"). Hypercalcemia can manifest as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, [increased thirst](Polydipsia "Polydipsia"), [frequent urination](Polyuria "Polyuria"), and altered mental status.[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7) Those with lung cancer also commonly experience [hypokalemia](Hypokalemia "Hypokalemia") (low potassium) due to inappropriate secretion of [adrenocorticotropic hormone](Adrenocorticotropic_hormone "Adrenocorticotropic hormone"), as well as [hyponatremia](Hyponatremia "Hyponatremia") (low sodium) due to overproduction of [antidiuretic hormone](Antidiuretic_hormone "Antidiuretic hormone") or [atrial natriuretic peptide](Atrial_natriuretic_peptide "Atrial natriuretic peptide").[[7]](Lung_cancer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-7) About one of three people with lung cancer develop [nail clubbing](Nail_clubbing "

### Incidence of a second cancer in survivors

In the developed world, one in three people will develop cancer during their lifetimes. If all cancer patients survived and cancer occurred randomly, the normal lifetime odds of developing a second primary cancer (not the first cancer spreading to a new site) would be one in nine.[[29]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Rheingold03-29) However, [cancer survivors](Cancer_survivor "Cancer survivor") have an increased risk of developing a second primary cancer, and the odds are about one in 4.5.[[29]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Rheingold03-29) About half of these second primaries can be attributed to the normal one-in-nine risk associated with random chance.[[29]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Rheingold03-29)

The increased risk is believed to be primarily due to the same risk factors that produced the first cancer, such as the person's genetic profile, alcohol and tobacco use, obesity, and environmental exposures, and partly due, in some cases, to the treatment for the first cancer, which might have included mutagenic chemotherapeutic drugs or radiation.[[29]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Rheingold03-29) Cancer survivors may also be more likely to comply with recommended screening, and thus may be more likely than average to detect cancers.[[29]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Rheingold03-29)

## Children

[Childhood cancer](Childhood_cancer "Childhood cancer") and cancer in adolescents is rare (about 150 cases per million yearly in the US). <Leukemia> (usually [acute lymphoblastic leukemia](Acute_lymphoblastic_leukemia "Acute lymphoblastic leukemia")) is the most common cancer in children aged 1–14 in the U.S., followed by the [central nervous system cancers](Brain_tumor "Brain tumor"), [neuroblastoma](Neuroblastoma "Neuroblastoma"), [Wilms' tumor](Wilms'_tumor "Wilms' tumor"), and [non-Hodgkin's lymphoma](Non-Hodgkin's_lymphoma "Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma").[[20]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-Jemal-20) Statistics from the SEER program of the US [NCI](National_Cancer_Institute "National Cancer Institute") demonstrate that childhood cancers increased 19% between 1975 and 1990, mainly due to an increased incidence in acute leukemia. Since 1990, incidence rates have decreased.[[30]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-SEER1999-30)

## Infants

The age of peak incidence of cancer in children occurs during the first year of life, in [infants](Infant "Infant"). The average annual incidence in the United States, 1975–1995, was 233 per million infants.[[30]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-SEER1999-30) Several estimates of incidence exist. According to SEER,[[30]](Epidemiology_of_cancer#cite_note-SEER1999-30) in the United States:

Based on my research through Wikipedia articles, here is what I found regarding 5-year survival rates for lung cancer worldwide, particularly for females:

## General Lung Cancer Survival Rates

**Global 5-Year Survival Rate**: 10-20% (most countries)
- According to the latest statistics from 2020, there were 2.2 million new lung cancer cases worldwide with 1.8 million deaths

## Gender-Specific Survival Data

### Key Finding: Women Have Better Survival Outcomes
The Lung cancer Wikipedia article explicitly states that "**Survival rates are higher in women compared to men**" for lung cancer. This is attributed to several factors including:
- Women are often diagnosed at an earlier stage
- Women tend to be diagnosed at a younger age
- Biological differences may play a role

### Small-Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) Specific Gender Breakdown
For small-cell lung cancer specifically (the more aggressive form, representing about 15% of cases):
- **10-Year Relative Survival Rate**: 3.5% overall
  - **Women: 4.3%**
  - **Men: 2.8%**

This data clearly shows women have significantly better survival outcomes for small-cell lung cancer.

### Regional Data (Australia)
Australia provides additional perspective on gender differences:
- 2018 deaths: 3,969 females vs. 5,229 males
- Overall survival rates improved from 9.2% to 17% (as of 2014)
- Risk of dying from lung cancer by age 85 is 1 in 23 overall, more likely in men than women

## Summary

While comprehensive worldwide 5-year survival statistics broken down by gender for general lung cancer are not universally available in the current data, the evidence consistently shows that:

1. **Overall lung cancer 5-year survival**: 10-20% globally
2. **Female advantage**: Women consistently show better survival rates than men
3. **For small-cell lung cancer specifically**: Women have a 4.3% 10-year survival rate vs. 2.8% for men (54% better)
4. **Australia example**: 17% overall survival rate as of 2014, with better outcomes for women

The improved survival for women may be due to earlier diagnosis, younger age at diagnosis, and potentially biological differences in how women's bodies respond to treatment and the disease progression.

## Signs and symptoms

The early stages of cervical cancer may be completely [free of symptoms](Asymptomatic "Asymptomatic").[[5]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Robbins-5)[[24]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid10735343-24) [Vaginal bleeding](Vaginal_bleeding "Vaginal bleeding"), contact bleeding (one most common form being bleeding after sexual intercourse), or (rarely) a vaginal mass may indicate the presence of malignancy. Also, moderate pain during sexual intercourse and vaginal discharge are symptoms of cervical cancer.[[27]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-27) In advanced disease, [metastases](Metastasis "Metastasis") may be present in the [abdomen](Abdomen "Abdomen"), [lungs](Lung "Lung"), or elsewhere.[[28]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-28)

Symptoms of advanced cervical cancer may include: [loss of appetite](Anorexia_(symptom) "Anorexia (symptom)"), weight loss, fatigue, pelvic pain, back pain, leg pain, swollen legs, heavy vaginal bleeding, bone fractures, and (rarely) leakage of urine or feces from the vagina.[[29]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-MedLine_Plus_Cerv_Cancer-29) Bleeding after douching or after a pelvic exam is a common symptom of cervical cancer.[[30]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-30)

## Causes

Infection with some types of HPV is the greatest risk factor for cervical cancer, followed by smoking.[[31]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-GadducciBarsotti2011-31) <HIV> infection is also a risk factor.[[31]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-GadducciBarsotti2011-31) Not all of the causes of cervical cancer are known, however, and several other contributing factors have been implicated.[[32]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-32)[[33]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-33)

### Human papillomavirus

[HPV](Human_papillomavirus_infection "Human papillomavirus infection") types 16 and 18 are the cause of 75% of cervical cancer cases globally, while 31 and 45 are the causes of another 10%.[[34]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-34)

Women who have multiple sexual partners, or have partners who have multiple sexual partners, regardless of sex are at higher risk of cervical cancer .[[35]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-ACS_What_Causes-35)[[36]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid11392939-36)

Of the 150-200 types of HPV known,[[37]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-MDL_HPV_Type-Detect-37)[[38]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NCI:Primer_on_HPV-38) 15 are classified as high-risk types (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 68, 73, and 82), three as probable high-risk (26, 53, and 66), and 12 as low-risk (6, 11, 40, 42, 43, 44, 54, 61, 70, 72, 81, and CP6108).[[39]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid12571259-39)

[Genital warts](Genital_wart "Genital wart"), which are a form of [benign tumor](Benign_tumor "Benign tumor") of [epithelial](Epithelium "Epithelium") cells, are also caused by various strains of HPV. However, these serotypes are usually not related to cervical cancer. Having multiple strains at the same time is common, including those that can cause cervical cancer along with those that cause warts. Infection with HPV is generally believed to be required for cervical cancer to occur.[[40]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid16362994-40)

### Smoking

Cigarette smoking, both active and passive, increases the risk of cervical cancer. Among HPV-infected women, current and former smokers have roughly two to three times the incidence of invasive cancer. Passive smoking is also associated with increased risk, but to a lesser extent.[[41]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NIHNCIHPV2015-41)

Smoking has also been linked to the development of cervical cancer.[[42]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-LuhnWalker2013-42)[[43]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-RemschmidtKaufmann2013-43)[[31]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-GadducciBarsotti2011-31) Smoking can increase the risk in women a few different ways, which can be by direct and indirect methods of inducing cervical cancer.[[42]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-LuhnWalker2013-42)[[31]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-GadducciBarsotti2011-31)[[44]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-AgorastosMiliaras2005-44) A direct way of contracting this cancer is a smoker has a higher chance of [cervical intraepithelial neoplasia](Cervical_intraepithelial_neoplasia "Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia") (CIN3) occurring, which has the potential of forming cervical cancer.[[42]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-LuhnWalker2013-42) When CIN3 lesions lead to cancer, most of them have the assistance of the HPV virus, but that is not always the case, which is why it can be considered a direct link to cervical cancer.[[44]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-AgorastosMiliaras2005-44) Heavy smoking and long-term smoking seem to have more of a risk of getting the CIN3 lesions than lighter smoking or not smoking at all.[[45]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-JensenSchmiedel2012-45) Although smoking has been linked to cervical cancer, it aids in the development of HPV, which is the leading cause of this type of cancer.[[31]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-GadducciBarsotti2011-31) Also, not only does it aid in the development of HPV, but also if the woman is already HPV-positive, she is at an even greater likelihood of contracting cervical cancer.[[45]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-JensenSchmiedel2012-45)

### Oral contraceptives

Long-term use of oral contraceptives is associated with increased risk of cervical cancer in women who have had [HPV](Human_papillomavirus_infection "Human papillomavirus infection"). Women who have used oral contraceptives for 5 to 9 years have about three times the incidence of invasive cancer, and those who used them for 10 years or longer have about four times the risk.[[41]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NIHNCIHPV2015-41)

### Multiple pregnancies

Having many pregnancies is associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer. Among HPV-infected women, those who have had seven or more full-term pregnancies have around four times the risk of cancer compared with women with no pregnancies, and two to three times the risk of women who have had one or two full-term pregnancies.[[41]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NIHNCIHPV2015-41)

## Diagnosis

### Biopsy

The [Pap test](Pap_test "Pap test") can be used as a [screening test](Screening_(medicine) "Screening (medicine)"), but produces a [false negative](False_positives_and_false_negatives#False_negative_error "False positives and false negatives") in up to 50% of cases of cervical cancer.[[46]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-46)[[47]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-47) Other concerns is the cost of doing Pap tests, which make them unaffordable in many areas of the world.[[48]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-48)

Confirmation of the diagnosis of cervical cancer or precancer requires a biopsy of the cervix. This is often done through [colposcopy](Colposcopy "Colposcopy"), a magnified visual inspection of the cervix aided by using a dilute [acetic acid](Acetic_acid "Acetic acid") (e.g. [vinegar](Vinegar "Vinegar")) solution to highlight abnormal cells on the surface of the cervix,[[5]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Robbins-5) with visual contrast provided by staining the normal tissues a mahogany brown with Lugol's iodine.[[49]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-49) Medical devices used for biopsy of the cervix include [punch forceps](Instruments_used_in_obstetrics_and_gynecology "Instruments used in obstetrics and gynecology"). Colposcopic impression, the estimate of disease severity based on the visual inspection, forms part of the diagnosis. Further diagnostic and treatment procedures are [loop electrical excision procedure](Loop_electrical_excision_procedure "Loop electrical excision procedure") and [cervical conization](Cervical_conization "Cervical conization"), in which the inner lining of the cervix is removed to be examined pathologically. These are carried out if the biopsy confirms severe [cervical intraepithelial neoplasia](Cervical_intraepithelial_neoplasia "Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia").

Often before the biopsy, the doctor asks for medical imaging to rule out other causes of woman's symptoms. Imaging modalities such as [ultrasound](Ultrasound "Ultrasound"), CT scan, and MRI have been used to look for alternating disease, spread of the tumor, and effect on adjacent structures. Typically, they appear as heterogeneous mass on the cervix.[[50]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-50)

- [Small cell carcinoma](Small_cell_carcinoma "Small cell carcinoma")
- [Neuroendocrine tumour](Neuroendocrine_tumour "Neuroendocrine tumour")
- [Glassy cell carcinoma](Glassy_cell_carcinoma_of_the_cervix "Glassy cell carcinoma of the cervix")

## Prevention

### Screening

Main articles: [Cervical screening](Cervical_screening "Cervical screening") and [Pap test](Pap_test "Pap test")

Checking cervical cells with the [Papanicolaou test](Pap_test "Pap test") (Pap test) for cervical pre-cancer has dramatically reduced the number of cases of, and mortality from, cervical cancer.[[24]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid10735343-24) Liquid-based cytology may reduce the number of inadequate samples.[[61]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-61)[[62]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-62)[[63]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-63) Pap test screening every three to five years with appropriate follow-up can reduce cervical cancer incidence up to 80%.[[64]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Arbyn10-64) Abnormal results may suggest the presence of [precancerous changes](Cervical_intraepithelial_neoplasia "Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia"), allowing examination and possible preventive treatment, known as [colposcopy](Colposcopy "Colposcopy"). The treatment of low-grade lesions may adversely affect subsequent fertility and pregnancy.[[41]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NIHNCIHPV2015-41) Personal invitations encouraging women to get screened are effective at increasing the likelihood they will do so. Educational materials also help increase the likelihood women will go for screening, but they are not as effective as invitations.[[65]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-65)

According to the 2010 European guidelines, the age at which to start screening ranges between 20 and 30 years of age, but preferentially not before age 25 or 30 years, and depends on burden of the disease in the population and the available resources.[[64]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Arbyn10-64)

In the United States, screening is recommended to begin at age 21, regardless of age at which a woman began having sex or other risk factors.[[66]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-USAScreen2014-66) Pap tests should be done every three years between the ages of 21 and 65.[[66]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-USAScreen2014-66) In women over the age of 65, screening may be discontinued if no abnormal screening results were seen within the previous 10 years and no history of CIN2 or higher exists.[[66]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-USAScreen2014-66)[[67]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Committee38-67)[[68]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Kar2013-68) HPV vaccination status does not change screening rates.[[67]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Committee38-67)

A number of recommended options exist for screening those 30 to 65.[[69]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-USPSTF2018-69) This includes cervical cytology every 3 years, HPV testing every 5 years, or HPV testing together with cytology every 5 years.[[69]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-USPSTF2018-69)[[67]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Committee38-67) Screening is not beneficial before age 25, as the rate of disease is low. Screening is not beneficial in women older than 60 years if they have a history of negative results.[[41]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NIHNCIHPV2015-41) The American Society of Clinical Oncology guideline has recommend for different levels of resource availability.[[70]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Primary_Prevention_of_Cervical_Canc-70)

Pap tests have not been as effective in developing countries.[[71]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-:0-71) This is in part because many of these countries have an impoverished health care infrastructure, too few trained and skilled professionals to obtain and interpret Pap tests, uninformed women who get lost to follow-up, and a lengthy turn-around time to get results.[[71]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-:0-71) Visual inspection with acetic acid and HPV DNA testing have been tried, though with mixed success.[[71]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-:0-71)

### Barrier protection

Barrier protection or spermicidal gel use during sexual intercourse decreases, but does not eliminate risk of transmitting the infection,[[41]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NIHNCIHPV2015-41) though condoms may protect against genital warts.[[72]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Manhart2002-72) They also provide protection against other sexually transmitted infections, such as [HIV](HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") and *[Chlamydia](Chlamydia_infection "Chlamydia infection")*, which are associated with greater risks of developing cervical cancer.

### Vaccination

Three [HPV vaccines](HPV_vaccines "HPV vaccines") (<Gardasil>, Gardasil 9, and <Cervarix>) reduce the risk of cancerous or precancerous changes of the cervix and [perineum](Perineum "Perineum") by about 93% and 62%, respectively.[[73]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Vaccine09-73) The vaccines are between 92% and 100% effective against HPV 16 and 18 up to at least 8 years.[[41]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-NIHNCIHPV2015-41)

HPV vaccines are typically given to age 9 to 26, as the vaccine is most effective if given before infection occurs. The duration of effectiveness and whether a booster will be needed is unknown. The high cost of this vaccine has been a cause for concern. Several countries have considered (or are considering) programs to fund HPV vaccination. The American Society of Clinical Oncology guideline has recommendations for different levels of resource availability.[[70]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Primary_Prevention_of_Cervical_Canc-70)

Since 2010, young women in Japan have been eligible to receive the cervical cancer vaccination for free.[[74]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Japan2013-74) In June 2013, the Japanese [Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare](Ministry_of_Health%2C_Labor_and_Welfare_(Japan) "Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare (Japan)") mandated that, before administering the vaccine, medical institutions must inform women that the ministry does not recommend it.[[74]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Japan2013-74) However, the vaccine is still available at no cost to Japanese women who choose to accept the vaccination.[[74]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Japan2013-74)

### Nutrition

[Vitamin A](Vitamin_A "Vitamin A") is associated with a lower risk[[75]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-75) as are [vitamin B12](Vitamin_B12 "Vitamin B12"), [vitamin C](Vitamin_C "Vitamin C"), [vitamin E](Vitamin_E "Vitamin E"), and [beta-Carotene](Beta-Carotene "Beta-Carotene").[[76]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-76)

The treatment of cervical cancer varies worldwide, largely due to access to surgeons skilled in radical pelvic surgery, and the emergence of fertility-sparing therapy in developed nations. Less advanced stages of cervical cancer typically have treatment options that allow fertility to be maintained, if the patient desires.[[77]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-77) Because cervical cancers are radiosensitive, radiation may be used in all stages where surgical options do not exist. Surgical intervention may have better outcomes than radiological approaches.[[78]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-BaalbergenVeenstra2013-78) In addition, chemotherapy can be used to treat cervical cancer, and has been found to be more effective than radiation alone.[[79]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-79) Evidence suggests chemoradiotherapy may increase overall survival and reduce the risk of disease recurrence compared to radiotherapy alone.[[80]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-80) There is low-certainty evidence that peri-operative care approaches, such as 'fast-track surgery' or 'enhanced recovery programmes' may lower surgical stress and improve recovery after gynaecological cancer surgery.[[81]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-81)

Microinvasive cancer (stage IA) may be treated by [hysterectomy](Hysterectomy "Hysterectomy") (removal of the whole uterus including part of the [vagina](Vagina "Vagina")).[[82]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-82) For stage IA2, the [lymph nodes](Lymph_node "Lymph node") are removed as well. Alternatives include local surgical procedures such as a [loop electrical excision procedure](Loop_electrical_excision_procedure "Loop electrical excision procedure")  or [cone biopsy](Cervical_conization "Cervical conization").[[83]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-83)[[84]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-LinZhou2017-84) A systematic review concluded that more evidence is needed to inform decisions about different surgical techniques for women with cervical cancer at stage IA2.[[85]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-85)

It is a viable option for those in stage I cervical cancer which has not spread; however, it is not yet considered a standard of care,[[88]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid16493253-88) as few doctors are skilled in this procedure. Even the most experienced surgeon cannot promise that a trachelectomy can be performed until after surgical microscopic examination, as the extent of the spread of cancer is unknown. If the surgeon is not able to microscopically confirm clear margins of cervical tissue once the woman is under general anesthesia in the operating room, a hysterectomy may still be needed. This can only be done during the same operation if the woman has given prior consent. Due to the possible risk of cancer spread to the lymph nodes in stage 1B cancers and some stage 1A cancers, the surgeon may also need to remove some lymph nodes from around the uterus for pathologic evaluation.

A radical trachelectomy can be performed abdominally[[89]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid15918265-89) or vaginally[[90]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid15936061-90) and opinions are conflicting as to which is better.[[91]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid8812529-91) A radical abdominal trachelectomy with lymphadenectomy usually only requires a two- to three-day hospital stay, and most women recover very quickly (about six weeks).
