Complications are uncommon, although women who are able to conceive after surgery are susceptible to preterm labor and possible late miscarriage.[[92]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid10760765-92) A wait of at least one year is generally recommended before attempting to become pregnant after surgery.[[93]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid12548192-93) Recurrence in the residual cervix is very rare if the cancer has been cleared with the trachelectomy.[[88]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid16493253-88) Yet, women are recommended to practice vigilant prevention and follow-up care including Pap screenings/[colposcopy](Colposcopy "Colposcopy"), with biopsies of the remaining lower uterine segment as needed (every 3–4 months for at least 5 years) to monitor for any recurrence in addition to minimizing any new exposures to HPV through [safe sex](Safe_sex "Safe sex") practices until one is actively trying to conceive.

Early stages (IB1 and IIA less than 4 cm) can be treated with radical hysterectomy with removal of the lymph nodes or [radiation therapy](Radiation_therapy "Radiation therapy"). Radiation therapy is given as external beam radiotherapy to the pelvis and [brachytherapy](Brachytherapy "Brachytherapy") (internal radiation). Women treated with surgery who have high-risk features found on pathologic examination are given radiation therapy with or without chemotherapy to reduce the risk of relapse. A Cochrane review has found moderate-certainty evidence that radiation decreases the risk of disease progression in people with stage IB cervical cancer, when compared to no further treatment.[[94]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Rogers_2012-94) However, little evidence was found on its effects on overall survival.[[94]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Rogers_2012-94)

Larger early-stage tumors (IB2 and IIA more than 4 cm) may be treated with radiation therapy and [cisplatin](Cisplatin "Cisplatin")-based chemotherapy, hysterectomy (which then usually requires [adjuvant](Adjuvant "Adjuvant") radiation therapy), or cisplatin chemotherapy followed by hysterectomy. When cisplatin is present, it is thought to be the most active single agent in periodic diseases.[[95]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-95) Such addition of platinum-based chemotherapy to chemoradiation seems not only to improve survival but also reduces risk of recurrence in women with early stage cervical cancer (IA2–IIA).[[96]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-96) A Cochrane review found a lack of evidence on the benefits and harms of primary hysterectomy compared to primary chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer in stage IB2.[[97]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-97)

Advanced-stage tumors (IIB-IVA) are treated with radiation therapy and cisplatin-based chemotherapy. On 15 June 2006, the US [Food and Drug Administration](Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") approved the use of a combination of two chemotherapy drugs, [hycamtin](Hycamtin "Hycamtin") and cisplatin, for women with late-stage (IVB) cervical cancer treatment.[[98]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-98) Combination treatment has significant risk of [neutropenia](Neutropenia "Neutropenia"), [anemia](Anemia "Anemia"), and [thrombocytopenia](Thrombocytopenia "Thrombocytopenia") side effects.[[99]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-99)

There is insufficient evidence whether anticancer drugs after standard care help women with locally advanced cervical cancer to live longer.[[100]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-100)

For surgery to be curative, the entire cancer must be removed with no cancer found at the margins of the removed tissue on examination under a microscope.[[101]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Sar2015-101) This procedure is known as exenteration.[[101]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Sar2015-101)

No evidence is available to suggest that any form of follow‐up approach is better or worse in terms of prolonging survival, improving quality of life or guiding the management of problems that can arise because of the treatment and that in the case of radiotherapy treatment worsen with time.[[102]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-102) A 2019 review found no controlled trials regarding the efficacy and safety of interventions for vaginal bleeding in women with advanced cervical cancer.[[103]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-103)

[Tisotumab vedotin](Tisotumab_vedotin "Tisotumab vedotin") (Tivdak) was approved for medical use in the United States in September 2021.[[104]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Tivdak_FDA_label-104)[[105]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Seagen_PR-105)

- Diagram showing the area removed with a posterior surgery

- Diagram showing the area removed with a total operation

- Diagram showing the area removed with an anterior operation

## Prognosis

### Stage

Prognosis depends on the stage of the cancer. For intraepithelial cervical neoplasmas the prognosis is good.[[106]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-106) With treatment, the five-year [relative survival rate](Relative_survival_rate "Relative survival rate") for the earliest stage of invasive cervical cancer is 92%, and the overall (all stages combined) five-year survival rate is about 66%. These statistics may be improved when applied to women newly diagnosed, bearing in mind that these outcomes may be partly based on the state of treatment five years ago when the women studied were first diagnosed.[[107]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-ACS_Key_Stats-107)

With treatment, 80–90% of women with stage I cancer and 60–75% of those with stage II cancer are alive 5 years after diagnosis. Survival rates decrease to 58% for women with stage III cancer and 17% or fewer of those with stage IV cancer five years after diagnosis.[[107]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-ACS_Key_Stats-107) Recurrent cervical cancer detected at its earliest stages might be successfully treated with surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or a combination of the three. About 35% of women with invasive cervical cancer have persistent or recurrent disease after treatment.[[108]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-AMN-108)

### By country

Five-year survival in the United States for [White women](White_people "White people") is 69% and for [Black women](Black_people "Black people") is 57%.[[109]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-109)

Regular screening has meant that precancerous changes and early-stage cervical cancers have been detected and treated early. Figures suggest that cervical screening is saving 5,000 lives each year in the UK by preventing cervical cancer.[[110]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-chelp-110) About 1,000 women per year die of cervical cancer in the UK. All of the [Nordic countries](Nordic_countries "Nordic countries") have cervical cancer-screening programs in place.[[111]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Nygard2011-111) The Pap test was integrated into clinical practice in the Nordic countries in the 1960s.[[111]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Nygard2011-111)

In Africa outcomes are often worse as diagnosis is frequently at a latter stage of disease.[[112]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-112) In a scoping review of publicly-available cervical cancer prevention and control plans from African countries, plans tended to emphasize survivorship rather than early HPV diagnosis and prevention.[[113]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-113)

## Epidemiology

Worldwide, cervical cancer is both the fourth-most common cause of cancer and deaths from cancer in women.[[3]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014-3) In 2018, 570,000 cases of cervical cancer were estimated to have occurred, with over 300,000 deaths.[[115]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-115) It is the second-most common cause of female-specific cancer after [breast cancer](Breast_cancer "Breast cancer"), accounting for around 8% of both total cancer cases and total cancer deaths in women.[[21]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014Total-21) About 80% of cervical cancers occur in developing countries.[[116]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Kent2010-116) It is the most frequently detected cancer during pregnancy, with an occurrence of 1.5 to 12 for every 100,000 pregnancies.[[117]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-CordeiroGemignani2017-117)

### Australia

In 2022, it is estimated that 942 new cases of cervical cancer will be diagnosed in Australia. In 2022, it is estimated that a female has a 1 in 180 (or 0.56%) risk of being diagnosed with cervical cancer by the age of 85.[[118]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-118)

In 2020, there were 165 women aged 25–74 who died from cervical cancer, which is a mortality rate of 2 deaths per 100,000 women in the population. Over the 5 years 2016–2020, there were 62 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women aged 25–74 who died from cervical cancer, which is a mortality rate of 7 deaths per 100,000 Indigenous women in the population. Over the 5 years 2016–2020, the age-standardised mortality rate among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women was 3.8 times the rate of non-Indigenous Australians.[[119]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-119)

The number of women diagnosed with cervical cancer has dropped on average by 4.5% each year since organised screening began in 1991 (1991–2005).[[120]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-120) Regular twice-yearly Pap tests can reduce the incidence of cervical cancer up to 90% in Australia, and save 1,200 Australian women from dying from the disease each year.[[121]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-121) It is predicted that because of the success of the primary HPV testing programme there will be fewer than four new cases per 100 000 women annually by 2028.[[122]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid30291040-122)

### Canada

An estimated 1,450 Canadians will be diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2022. An estimated 380 will die from it.[[123]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-123)

### India

In India, the number of people with cervical cancer is rising, but overall the age-adjusted rates are decreasing.[[124]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-124) Usage of condoms in the female population has improved the survival of women with cancers of the cervix.[[125]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-125)

### European Union

As of 2022, the World Health Organization announced that "each year in the WHO European Region more than 66 000 women are newly diagnosed with cervical cancer and more than 30 000 die from this preventable disease. "[[126]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-126)

### United Kingdom

Cervical cancer is the 12th-most common cancer in women in the UK (around 3,100 women were diagnosed with the disease in 2011), and accounts for 1% of cancer deaths (around 920 died in 2012).[[127]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-127) With a 42% reduction from 1988 to 1997, the NHS-implemented screening programme has been highly successful, screening the highest-risk age group (25–49 years) every 3 years, and those ages 50–64 every 5 years.

### United States

An estimated 13,170 new cervical cancers and 4,250 cervical cancer deaths will occur in the United States in 2019.[[128]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-128) The median age at diagnosis is 50. The rates of new cases in the United States was 7.3 per 100,000 women, based on rates from 2012 to 2016. Cervical cancer deaths decreased by approximately 74% in the last 50 years, largely due to widespread Pap test screening.[[129]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Armstrong10-129) The annual direct medical cost of cervical cancer prevention and treatment prior to introduction of the HPV vaccine was estimated at $6 billion.[[129]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Armstrong10-129)

### Nigeria

The Nigerian Institute of Medical Research (NIMR) reports that 28 Nigerian women lose their lives daily due to this disease. This alarming statistic underscores the pressing need for better awareness, prevention, and treatment efforts across the country. Numerous Nigerian women lack access to these preventive measures. In many regions of the country, screening tests such as Pap tests and HPV tests are not easily accessible or affordable[[130]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-130)[[131]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-131)

## History

- 400 BCE: <Hippocrates> noted that cervical cancer was incurable.
- 1925: Hinselmann invented the [colposcope](Colposcope "Colposcope").
- 1928: [Papanicolaou](Georgios_Papanikolaou "Georgios Papanikolaou") developed the Papanicolaou technique.
- 1941: Papanicolaou and Traut: [Pap test](Pap_test "Pap test") screening began.
- 1946: [Aylesbury spatula](Aylesbury_spatula "Aylesbury spatula") was developed to scrape the cervix, collecting the sample for the Pap test.
- 1951: First successful in-vitro cell line, <HeLa>, derived from biopsy of cervical cancer of [Henrietta Lacks](Henrietta_Lacks "Henrietta Lacks").
- 1976: [Harald zur Hausen](Harald_zur_Hausen "Harald zur Hausen") and Gisam found HPV DNA in cervical cancer and genital warts; Hausen later won the [Nobel Prize](Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine") for his work.[[132]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-zur2002-132)
- 1988: [Bethesda System](Bethesda_System "Bethesda System") for reporting Pap results was developed.
- 2006: First [HPV vaccine](HPV_vaccine "HPV vaccine") was approved by the FDA.
- 2015: HPV Vaccine shown to protect against infection at multiple body sites.[[133]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-133)
- 2018: Evidence for single-dose protection with HPV vaccine.[[134]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-134)


[Epidemiologists](Epidemiology "Epidemiology") working in the early 20th century noted that cervical cancer behaved like a sexually transmitted disease. In summary:

1. Cervical cancer was noted to be common in female [sex workers](Sex_worker "Sex worker").
2. It was rare in [nuns](Nun "Nun"), except for those who had been sexually active before entering the convent (Rigoni in 1841).
3. It was more common in the second wives of men whose first wives had died from cervical cancer.
4. It was rare in Jewish women.[[135]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid12674663-135)
5. In 1935, Syverton and Berry discovered a relationship between RPV (Rabbit Papillomavirus) and skin cancer in [rabbits](Rabbit "Rabbit") (HPV is species-specific and therefore cannot be transmitted to rabbits).


These historical observations suggested that cervical cancer could be caused by a sexually transmitted agent. Initial research in the 1940s and 1950s attributed cervical cancer to [smegma](Smegma "Smegma") (e.g. Heins *et al.* 1958).[[136]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-Heins1958-136) During the 1960s and 1970s it was suspected that infection with [herpes simplex virus](Herpes_simplex_virus "Herpes simplex virus") was the cause of the disease. In summary, [HSV](Herpes_simplex_virus "Herpes simplex virus") was seen as a likely cause because it is known to survive in the female reproductive tract, to be transmitted sexually in a way compatible with known risk factors, such as promiscuity and low socioeconomic status.[[137]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid4352386-137) Herpes viruses were also implicated in other malignant diseases, including [Burkitt's lymphoma](Burkitt's_lymphoma "Burkitt's lymphoma"), [Nasopharyngeal carcinoma](Nasopharyngeal_carcinoma "Nasopharyngeal carcinoma"), [Marek's disease](Marek's_disease "Marek's disease") and the Lucké renal adenocarcinoma. HSV was recovered from cervical tumour cells.

A description of [human papillomavirus](Human_papillomavirus "Human papillomavirus") (HPV) by [electron microscopy](Electron_microscopy "Electron microscopy") was given in 1949, and HPV-DNA was identified in 1963.[[138]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-138) It was not until the 1980s that HPV was identified in cervical cancer tissue.[[139]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid6304740-139) It has since been demonstrated that HPV is implicated in virtually all cervical cancers.[[140]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-pmid16670757-140) Specific viral subtypes implicated are HPV 16, 18, 31, 45 and others.

In work that was initiated in the mid-1980s, the HPV vaccine was developed, in parallel, by researchers at [Georgetown University](Georgetown_University "Georgetown University") Medical Center, the [University of Rochester](University_of_Rochester "University of Rochester"), the [University of Queensland](University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland") in Australia, and the U.S. [National Cancer Institute](National_Cancer_Institute "National Cancer Institute").[[141]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-141) In 2006, the [U.S. Food and Drug Administration](Food_and_Drug_Administration_(United_States) "Food and Drug Administration (United States)") (FDA) approved the first preventive HPV vaccine, marketed by [Merck & Co.](Merck_%26_Co. "Merck & Co.") under the trade name Gardasil.

In November 2020, the [World Health Organization](World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization"), under backing from the [World Health Assembly](World_Health_Assembly "World Health Assembly"), set out a strategy to eliminate cervical cancer by 2050. The strategy involves vaccinating 90% of girls by the age of 15, screening 70% of women by the age of 35 and again by the age of 45, and treating 90% of women identified with cervical disease.[[142]](Cervical_cancer#cite_note-142)

Based on the Wikipedia article for Cervical Cancer, here is the comprehensive information about 5-year survival rates worldwide:

## 5-Year Survival Rates by Stage

| Stage | Survival Rate |
|-------|---------------|
| **Stage I** (earliest invasive cancer) | 92% |
| **Stage I** (overall) | 80-90% |
| **Stage II** | 60-75% |
| **Stage III** | 58% |
| **Stage IV** | 17% or fewer |
| **All stages combined** | ~66% |

## 5-Year Survival Rates by Country

| Country/Population | Survival Rate |
|-------------------|---------------|
| **United States (overall)** | 68% |
| **United States (White women)** | 69% |
| **United States (Black women)** | 57% |
| **India** | 46% |

## Global Context

**Key Disparities:**
- About **80%** of cervical cancers occur in **developing countries**
- About **70%** of cervical cancers and **90%** of deaths occur in developing countries
- In **Africa**, outcomes are often worse as diagnosis is frequently at a later stage of disease
- In **low-income countries**, the incidence rate is 47.3 per 100,000 women

**Impact of Screening:**
- **United States**: Cervical cancer deaths decreased by approximately **74%** in the last 50 years, largely due to widespread Pap test screening
- **United Kingdom**: Screening program resulted in a **42%** reduction from 1988 to 1997
- Regular Pap tests can reduce cervical cancer incidence by up to **80-90%** when screening is implemented effectively

**Why Survival Rates Vary:**
Survival rates depend heavily on:
1. **Stage at diagnosis** (earlier detection = much better outcomes)
2. **Access to screening programs**
3. **Quality of healthcare infrastructure**
4. **Early treatment availability**

**Recent Statistics (2020):**
- **604,127** new cases worldwide
- **341,831** deaths

**Prevention Strategy (WHO, 2020):**
The World Health Organization set a goal to eliminate cervical cancer by 2050 through:
- 90% of girls vaccinated by age 15
- 70% of women screened by age 35 and again by age 45
- 90% of women with cervical disease treated

The dramatic difference between early-stage survival (92%) and overall survival (66%) highlights the critical importance of screening and early detection programs worldwide.

You are a helpful assistant. Current date: 11-20-2023.

# Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

## Writing Instructions

The instructions you give to each subagent SHOULD be a smaller piece of the instructions you were given. Do not delegate your full task to a subagent. Subagents do not have access to the information you have retrieved in prior turns or your thoughts. You must provide each subagent with the necessary context it needs in its instructions.

Your instructions to a subagent can be long, up to about 5000 characters. Each subagent is as capable as you are, but starts with a blank slate, so you must provide it specific and detailed information in its instructions.

Examples of poor instructions:
- Analyze the retrieved page to find the number of stations.
- Implement the `dfs()` function.
- Use the article to list the subway connections.
- Prove Lemma 3.
- Continue searching for the magic number.

[Cancer staging](Cancer_staging "Cancer staging") is the process of determining the extent of the development of a cancer. The [TNM staging system](TNM_staging_system "TNM staging system") is usually used to classify stages of cancers, but not of the brain.[[42]](Thyroid_cancer#cite_note-42)

Thyroid cancer can spread directly, via lymphatics or blood. Direct spread occurs through infiltration of the surrounding tissues. ## Prognosis

The prognosis of thyroid cancer is related to the type of cancer and the stage at the time of diagnosis. For the most common form of thyroid cancer, papillary, the overall prognosis is excellent. Indeed, the increased incidence of papillary thyroid carcinoma in recent years is likely related to increased and earlier diagnosis. One can look at the trend to earlier diagnosis in two ways. The first is that many of these cancers are small and not likely to develop into aggressive malignancies. A second perspective is that earlier diagnosis removes these cancers at a time when they are not likely to have spread beyond the thyroid gland, thereby improving the long-term outcome for the patient. No consensus exists at present on whether this trend toward earlier diagnosis is beneficial or unnecessary.

The argument against early diagnosis and treatment is based on the logic that many small thyroid cancers (mostly papillary) will not grow or metastasize. This view holds the overwhelming majority of thyroid cancers are [overdiagnosed](Overdiagnosed "Overdiagnosed") that is, will never cause any symptoms, illness, or death for the patient, even if nothing is ever done about the cancer. Including these overdiagnosed cases skews the statistics by lumping clinically significant cases in with apparently harmless cancers.[[54]](Thyroid_cancer#cite_note-Welch-54) Thyroid cancer is incredibly common, with [autopsy](Autopsy "Autopsy") studies of people dying from other causes showing that more than one-third of older adults technically have thyroid cancer, which is causing them no harm.[[54]](Thyroid_cancer#cite_note-Welch-54) Detecting nodules that might be cancerous is easy, simply by feeling the throat, which contributes to the level of overdiagnosis. Benign (noncancerous) nodules frequently co-exist with thyroid cancer; sometimes, a benign nodule is discovered, but surgery uncovers an incidental small thyroid cancer. Increasingly, small thyroid nodules are discovered as incidental findings on imaging (CT scan, MRI, ultrasound) performed for another purpose; very few of these people with accidentally discovered, symptom-free thyroid cancers will ever have any symptoms, and treatment in such patients has the potential to cause harm to them, not to help them.[[54]](Thyroid_cancer#cite_note-Welch-54)[[55]](Thyroid_cancer#cite_note-55)

**Colorectal cancer** (**CRC**), also known as **bowel cancer**, **colon cancer**, or **rectal cancer**, is the development of [cancer](Cancer "Cancer") from the [colon](Colon_(anatomy) "Colon (anatomy)") or [rectum](Rectum "Rectum") (parts of the [large intestine](Large_intestine "Large intestine")).[[5]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014PtTx-5) Signs and symptoms may include [blood in the stool](Lower_gastrointestinal_bleeding "Lower gastrointestinal bleeding"), a change in [bowel movements](Bowel_movements "Bowel movements"), weight loss, and fatigue.[[9]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-9) Most colorectal cancers are due to old age and lifestyle factors, with only a small number of cases due to underlying [genetic disorders](Genetic_disorder "Genetic disorder").[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2)[[3]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014Pre-3) Risk factors include diet, [obesity](Obesity "Obesity"), smoking, and lack of [physical activity](Physical_activity "Physical activity").[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2) Dietary factors that increase the risk include [red meat](Red_meat "Red meat"), [processed meat](Processed_meat "Processed meat"), and alcohol.[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2)[[4]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Theodoratou2017-4) Another risk factor is [inflammatory bowel disease](Inflammatory_bowel_disease "Inflammatory bowel disease"), which includes [Crohn's disease](Crohn's_disease "Crohn's disease") and [ulcerative colitis](Ulcerative_colitis "Ulcerative colitis").[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2) Some of the inherited genetic disorders that can cause colorectal cancer include [familial adenomatous polyposis](Familial_adenomatous_polyposis "Familial adenomatous polyposis") and [hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer](Hereditary_non-polyposis_colon_cancer "Hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer"); however, these represent less than 5% of cases.[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2)[[3]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014Pre-3) It typically starts as a [benign tumor](Adenoma "Adenoma"), often in the form of a [polyp](Colorectal_polyp "Colorectal polyp"), which over time becomes [cancerous](Carcinoma "Carcinoma").[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2)

Colorectal cancer may be diagnosed by [obtaining a sample](Biopsy "Biopsy") of the colon during a [sigmoidoscopy](Sigmoidoscopy "Sigmoidoscopy") or [colonoscopy](Colonoscopy "Colonoscopy").[[1]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014Pt-1) This is then followed by [medical imaging](Medical_imaging "Medical imaging") to determine whether the disease has spread.[[5]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014PtTx-5) [Screening](Cancer_screening "Cancer screening") is effective for preventing and decreasing deaths from colorectal cancer.[[10]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-USPSTF2016-10) Screening, by one of a number of methods, is recommended starting from the age of 45 to 75. It was recommended starting at age 50 but it was changed to 45 due to increasing amount of colon cancers.[[10]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-USPSTF2016-10)[[11]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-11) During colonoscopy, small polyps may be removed if found.[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2) If a large polyp or tumor is found, a [biopsy](Biopsy "Biopsy") may be performed to check if it is cancerous. <Aspirin> and other [non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs](Non-steroidal_anti-inflammatory_drugs "Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs") decrease the risk of pain during polyp excision.[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2)[[12]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-12) Their general use is not recommended for this purpose, however, due to side effects.[[13]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-13)

Treatments used for colorectal cancer may include some combination of surgery, [radiation therapy](Radiation_therapy "Radiation therapy"), [chemotherapy](Chemotherapy "Chemotherapy"), and [targeted therapy](Targeted_therapy "Targeted therapy").[[5]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014PtTx-5) Cancers that are confined within the wall of the colon may be curable with surgery, while [cancer that has spread widely](Metastasis "Metastasis") is usually not curable, with management being directed towards improving [quality of life](Quality_of_life "Quality of life") and symptoms.[[5]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014PtTx-5) The [five-year survival rate](Five-year_survival_rate "Five-year survival rate") in the United States was around 65% in 2014.[[6]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-SEER2014-6) The individual likelihood of survival depends on how advanced the cancer is, whether or not all the cancer can be removed with surgery, and the person's overall health.[[1]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-NCI2014Pt-1) Globally, colorectal cancer is the third most common type of cancer, making up about 10% of all cases.[[14]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014Epi-14) In 2018, there were 1.09 million new cases and 551,000 deaths from the disease.[[8]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Bray2018-8) It is more common in [developed countries](Developed_country "Developed country"), where more than 65% of cases are found.[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2) It is less common in women than men.[[2]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCR2014_5.5-2)

## Signs and symptoms

The signs and symptoms of colorectal cancer depend on the location of the [tumor](Tumor "Tumor") in the [bowel](Bowel "Bowel"), and whether it has spread elsewhere in the body ([metastasis](Metastasis "Metastasis")). The classic warning signs include: worsening [constipation](Constipation "Constipation"), blood in the [stool](Stool_test "Stool test"), decrease in stool caliber (thickness), loss of appetite, loss of weight, and [nausea](Nausea "Nausea") or [vomiting](Vomiting "Vomiting") in someone over 50 years old.[[15]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-15) Around 50% of people who have colorectal cancer do not report any symptoms.[[16]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-16)

[Rectal bleeding](Rectal_bleeding "Rectal bleeding") or [anemia](Anemia "Anemia") are high-risk symptoms in people over the age of 50.[[17]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Sym11-17) Weight loss and changes in a person's bowel habit are typically only concerning if they are associated with rectal bleeding.[[17]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Sym11-17)[[18]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-pmid21624112-18)

## Cause

75–95% of colorectal cancer cases occur in people with little or no genetic risk.[[19]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Cause11-19)[[20]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Lancet10-20) Risk factors include older age, male sex,[[20]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Lancet10-20) high intake of fat, [sugar](Sugar "Sugar"), [alcohol](Alcohol_(drug) "Alcohol (drug)"), [red meat](Red_meat "Red meat"), [processed meats](Processed_meat "Processed meat"), [obesity](Obesity "Obesity"), [smoking](Smoking "Smoking"), and a lack of [physical exercise](Physical_exercise "Physical exercise").[[19]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Cause11-19)[[21]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-WCRF2011-21) Approximately 10% of cases are linked to insufficient activity.[[22]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-22) The risk from alcohol appears to increase at greater than one drink per day.[[23]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Fedirko2011-23) Drinking five glasses of water a day is linked to a decrease in the risk of colorectal cancer and [adenomatous](Adenomatous "Adenomatous") polyps.[[24]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-24) *[Streptococcus gallolyticus](Streptococcus_gallolyticus "Streptococcus gallolyticus")* is associated with colorectal cancer.[[25]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-BoleijvanGelder2011-25) Some strains of *Streptococcus bovis/Streptococcus equinus* complex are consumed by millions of people daily and thus may be safe.[[26]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-JansMeile2015-26) 25 to 80% of people with *Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus* bacteremia have concomitant colorectal tumors.[[27]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-AbdulamirHafidh2011-27) Seroprevalence of *Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus* is considered as a candidate practical marker for the early prediction of an underlying bowel lesion at high risk population.[[27]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-AbdulamirHafidh2011-27) It has been suggested that the presence of antibodies to *Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus* antigens or the antigens themselves in the bloodstream may act as markers for the carcinogenesis in the colon.[[27]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-AbdulamirHafidh2011-27)

As with most other forms of cancer, tumor staging is based on the [TNM system](TNM_staging_system "TNM staging system") which considers how much the initial tumor has spread and the presence of metastases in lymph nodes and more distant organs.[[20]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-Lancet10-20) The AJCC 8th edition was published in 2018.[[85]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-85)

## Prevention

It has been estimated that about half of colorectal cancer cases are due to lifestyle factors, and about a quarter of all cases are preventable.[[86]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-86) Increasing surveillance, engaging in physical activity, consuming a diet high in fiber, and reducing smoking and alcohol consumption decrease the risk.[[87]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-87)[[88]](Colorectal_cancer#cite_note-88)

content:
Based on my search, I found detailed information about colon cancer prognosis and survival statistics on Wikipedia. Here's what I discovered:

## Overall Survival Rates

**United States**: The five-year survival rate for colorectal cancer was approximately **65%** (2014 data).

**Europe**: The five-year survival rate is **less than 60%**.

**Developed World**: About **one-third** of people who get colorectal cancer die from it.

## Survival Rates by Stage

Survival is directly related to detection stage, with early-stage survival rates about **five times higher** than late-stage cancers:

| Stage | Description | Five-Year Survival Rate |
|-------|-------------|------------------------|
| Tis, N0, M0 | Tumor hasn't breached muscularis mucosa | **100%** |
| T1 or T2 | Within submucosal or muscular layer | **~90%** |
| T3-4, N0, M0 | More invasive, no lymph node involvement | **~70%** |
| Any T, N1-3, M0 | Positive regional lymph nodes | **~40%** |
| Any T, any N, M1 | Distant metastases | **<5% to 31%** |

## Global Epidemiology

- **Global incidence varies 10-fold** worldwide
- **Highest rates**: Australia, New Zealand, Europe, and the United States
- **Lowest rates**: Africa and South-Central Asia
- **2018 statistics**: 1.09 million new cases and 551,000 deaths globally
- **Trend**: Colorectal cancer is more common in developed countries, where more than 65% of cases are found

### Regional Incidence Examples
- **United States**: ~151,000 cases annually (2022 estimate)
- **UK**: ~41,000 cases annually (fourth most common cancer)
- **Australia**: One in 19 men and one in 28 women develop it before age 75
- **Papua New Guinea**: Rare, estimated at 8 per 100,000 people annually
- **Disparity**: African Americans have 20% higher incidence and 40% higher mortality rates than other US racial/ethnic groups

## Key Prognostic Factors

The prognosis depends on:
- Physical fitness level of the patient
- Extent of metastases
- Tumor grade
- Stage at detection
- Treatment access and quality

The significant variation in survival rates across countries and regions is largely attributed to differences in screening programs, healthcare access, treatment availability, and stage at diagnosis.
